notes.meaning: Peter writes warmly to friends he calls "beloved." Both of his letters are reminders. He wants to wake up their sincere minds to truths they already know. He points them to two trusted voices: the Old Testament prophets, and the teaching of Jesus passed on by the apostles. Remembering these often keeps faith alive and active.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars think a later writer used Peter's name. They point to the phrase "your apostles" as a clue. Others answer that this reads too much into the words.

notes.meaning: Peter wants them to know ahead of time that mockers will come. These people laugh at God's promises and live however they please, following their own desires. Their real problem is the heart, not the mind: they do not want Jesus as Lord. The "last days" here means the age of the gospel, the time of Christ's kingdom.

differ.view: The "last days" are the whole time between Jesus' first coming and his return.
The "last days" are the days just before Christ comes back.
The phrase most likely points to the last days of the Jewish nation, which was soon to come to an end.

notes.meaning: The mockers ask, "Where is this promise that Jesus will come back?" They say the fathers have "fallen asleep," meaning they have died, and nothing has changed. Everything goes on as it always has. They set the steady order of nature against God's promise, as if God could never do anything new.

The mockers choose to forget something important. God made the heavens and the earth by his word, and the earth rose up out of water. Yet that same water later flooded the world in Noah's day, and that world perished. So it is simply not true that nothing has ever changed. The God who judged once can judge again.

By that same word, God now holds the present heavens and earth. They are stored up, kept for fire on Judgment Day, when ungodly people will be destroyed. The first world was judged by water; the next judgment will be by fire. Only God's word keeps everything going until his time comes.

Now Peter turns to the believers. God is not bound by time the way we are (see Psalm 90:4). A thousand years is nothing to him, and he can do a thousand years of work in one day. What feels like a long wait to us is no delay at all to God.

God is not slow, and he has not forgotten his promise. He keeps his own timetable. What looks like delay is really his patience, giving people time for repentance, which means turning from sin to God. God takes no joy in anyone being lost. This does not mean that everyone will in the end be saved.

differ.view: "You" means the believers, so God's patience waits until all whom he has chosen have come to repentance. The gospel invites everyone, but God draws to himself those he chose.
God truly wants every single person to be saved. He has never decided ahead of time that anyone must be lost, and he has made salvation possible for all.

notes.meaning: The Day of the Lord will come suddenly, like a thief, when people are not expecting it. The heavens will pass away with a roar, and fire will melt the elements. The earth and everything made on it will be exposed to the fire. All that sin brought into the world will be burned away, but for God's own works it will be a cleansing fire.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some of the oldest copies of this verse say the earth and its works "will be found" instead of "burned up." This is closer to the BSB's "laid bare." The exact wording here is hard to be sure of.

notes.meaning: If everything around us will one day pass away, how should we live? Peter says: in holy and godly ways, both toward other people and toward God. Believers should not dread that day but look forward to it eagerly. They can even "hasten" it, by longing for it, praying for Christ's coming, and spreading the gospel. This is a patient waiting, but never a lazy one.

The fire is not the end of the story. God has promised a new heaven and a new earth (Isaiah 65:17; 66:22). Righteousness will be at home there, with no sin at all. Many older Bible teachers believed this present world will be purified and made new, not simply wiped out.

So, while you wait, work hard to be ready when Jesus comes. Be at peace with God through Christ, with a quiet conscience, and at peace with others. Aim to be spotless and blameless in his eyes. No one is perfect yet, but this is the goal. Those who are in Christ will stand before him clothed in his goodness, not their own.

See the Lord's patience as a chance for people to be saved. Paul taught the same thing (see Romans 2:4). Peter calls him a "beloved brother," even though Paul had once corrected him in public. Peter admits some parts of Paul's letters are hard. Untaught and unsteady people twist them, as they twist the rest of Scripture, and it ruins them. Peter counts Paul's letters as Scripture. Hard parts are no reason to stop reading; we should come with a humble, teachable heart.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholic teaching has pointed to this verse to say that hard passages of Scripture should be understood with the guidance of the Church, not by each reader alone.

notes.meaning: You have been warned ahead of time, so stay on guard. Don't let the errors of lawless people carry you away. If you are swept along by false teaching, you lose your firm footing and become unsettled, like a wave tossed by the wind.

differ.view: The warning is meant to shake us out of laziness, not to shake our trust in God's promises. The danger is drifting from firm truth into error, not losing God's grace.
True believers can never finally fall away from salvation. But they can lose their steadiness and begin to doubt and waver.
This is a real warning not to fall from the faith in Christ that brought us God's grace. Believers must keep holding on to God and his word.

notes.meaning: The best way not to fall back is to keep growing. Grow in grace, which is God's undeserved kindness and the gifts he gives through Christ. And grow in knowing Jesus, so you become more like him and love him more. Peter ends by giving glory to Christ, now and forever, which shows that Jesus is God. Eternity is pictured as one endless day.
